lessonRef.title: Writing revise and edit: revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening within the unit “Opinion Writing: Reasons That Convince.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's writing revise and edit work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] At the small theater workshop, Jonah opened a folder containing an early draft beside the writer's published version. A note on the cover read “Opinion Writing: Reasons That Convince,” but the pages inside told one unfinished story. Jonah expected the ending to explain everything. Instead, the first scene offered only a quiet choice: return a borrowed object without comment or admit why it had been kept.

[2] The main character rehearsed an apology three times. In the first version, every sentence began with “I.” In the second, the character blamed the confusing rules. In the third, the character named the harm, returned the object, and then stopped talking. The narrator never announced which version was sincere.

[3] Nia noticed that a repeated image—a door left slightly open—appeared before each rehearsal. At first it seemed like background description. By its third appearance, the image could suggest an invitation, an escape, or an unfinished decision. The story gave enough detail to support more than one interpretation but not enough to make every interpretation equally strong.

[4] The final scene ended before the apology was delivered. Jonah argued that the missing speech made the character seem afraid; Nia thought the pause showed care. To connect the scene to revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening, each reader had to identify exact language, explain an inference, and account for the detail that made the other reading possible.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 121: revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 121: revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening,” then answer: Revisit your work on revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening. Which revision improves meaning, organization, or evidence most, and why?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a revised passage plus a revision note that identifies the change and its effect; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 121: revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 121: revising the conclusion so it does more than repeat the opening.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
